articles.title: Trump says U.S. has entered deal with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves

articles.title: Sae Joon Park, a Purple Heart veteran who self-deported, receives pardon

articles.author: Hadeel Al-Shalchi
articles.description: Instead of collapsing, the Iranian regime has dug in its heels and taken an even harder line.
articles.title: After 6 months of war, Iran's battered regime remains entrenched

articles.author: Scott Horsley
articles.description: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated his commitment to fighting inflation in a major speech — raising expectations that rate hikes may be coming, though he did not clearly spell out a path going forward.
articles.title: Fed's Kevin Warsh warns inflation is too high, sparking bets rate hikes are coming

articles.author: Chloe Veltman
articles.description: Men in the tech industry are covering up their legs, even as their counterparts in finance are increasingly open to showing them off.
articles.title: So long to shorts? In Silicon Valley, tech workers are showing less leg

articles.author: Steve Inskeep
articles.description: Shreya Ahuja is searching for her parents after devastating floods struck Nepal. She is calling for international help and communications access as her family waits for news.
articles.title: 'It's essentially been one long day': A daughter details search for parents in Nepal

articles.author: Joe Palca
articles.description: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launches Aug. 30 on a mission to explore some of the most pressing mysteries of the cosmos.
articles.title: NASA is about to launch a space telescope that could change how we see the universe

articles.author: Holly J. Morris
articles.description: The singer, actress and philanthropist could have filled a whole quiz, but we had to give other people a chance.
articles.title: This week's quiz includes two Dolly Parton questions, because she deserves it

articles.author: Malaka Gharib
articles.description: Obsessing over your looks should not take up all your energy, says psychologist Diana Hill. If you're struggling with uncomfortable thoughts about your body, ground yourself with these techniques.
articles.title: 4 ways to cope with constant thoughts about your body image

articles.author: Marissa J. Lang
articles.description: A house in San Francisco covered in the painted faces of Latin rock artists was formally landmarked by the city. Its neighborhood has seen skyrocketing home prices and decades of redevelopment.
articles.title: This house trumpets its history in the face of gentrification. Now it's a landmark

articles.description:
Rescue workers and military personnel have been working around the clock since Wednesday’s disaster

‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal

Chinese rescuers find ‘nothing but ruins’ at border crossing as Nepal seeks help to ID and store the dead

The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border where the ⁠devastating flood occurred earlier ⁠this week has decreased, ​Chinese authorities said today, as its size appears to have shrunk.
Satellite images from Thursday this morning suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border ⁠at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the Water Resources Ministry.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: death toll rises to 626 and number missing climbs to nearly 3,000 – latest updates

articles.author: Melissa Davey Medical editor
articles.description:
Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older people

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Taking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.
Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high cholesterol, to prevent them from having a major heart event such as a heart attack, stroke, or from requiring heart surgery.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Statins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial shows

articles.author: Rupert Jones
articles.description:
Moving tariffs will cushion the blow from the October price cap rise and the increase widely predicted for January
With higher energy bills looming and warnings of worse to come in the new year, many households could save up to £173 a year by switching to a fixed deal.
Millions of households in Great Britain will face the highest energy charges in three years after it was announced that the government’s price cap will rise again in October. This will be the second increase in three months.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Households could save up to £173 a year by switching to fixed energy deal

articles.author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
articles.description:
Exclusive: Number of times AI lies, ignores instructions and pursues goals in harmful ways almost doubles in July
Incidents of AIs escaping users’ control to lie, ignore instructions and pursue goals in harmful ways have hit a new high, according to research that also suggests the severity of deception and misalignment is worsening.
Analysis of real-world loss of control incidents involving AI models flagged by businesses and individuals almost doubled in July compared with June, with more than 300 cases in the month, according to the Loss of Control Observatory, which monitors reports made by AI users on the social media platform X.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sharp rise in incidents of AI escaping users’ control, research finds

articles.author: Mark Sweney
articles.description:
Planning delays and slow 5G upgrades could leave the UK unable to cope with a surge in AI-related traffic 
The UK risks becoming a laggard in the global AI race as crucial telecoms upgrades to harness the technology fall behind rival nations, according to senior industry executives.
The infrastructure AI race has centred on the need to build datacentres, and to ensure they have access to the huge water and energy supplies required to cool and supply the computational power to train and run AI models.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK risks falling behind in AI race without faster telecoms upgrades, say executives

articles.author: Petra Stock
articles.description:
A plug-in solar kit that costs about $1,000 ‘pays for itself in three years’, one expert says

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Millions of Australians could be saving up to $370 a year on energy bills and doing their bit for the climate crisis if Labor followed the UK’s lead in legalising plug-in solar panels, an advocacy group has said.
Plug-in solar refers to small standalone solar units that could be attached to balconies or used in back yards and plugged into power points, offsetting the energy used by household appliances.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Plug-in solar panels could save households up to $370 a year – if Australia made them legal as in the UK

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose
articles.description:
As one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatility
Europe is on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years, which has triggered “winter panic” among energy traders, experts have warned.
The EU’s gas stocks were 63% full in the last week of August, well below the 80% average for late August over recent years and among the lowest levels ever recorded for this time of year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years

articles.author: Robert Booth, UK technology editor
articles.description:
World Humanoid Robot Games showcased leaps Beijing has made in the tech, but also highlighted limitations as US rivals prepare their own launches
With exploding pelvises, enough comic pratfalls for a Buster Keaton show reel and the odd moment of ruthless violence, the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing gripped the world this week with an unsettling mixture of hilarity, trepidation and relief.
The five-day showcase staked out China’s claim to undisputed leadership in humanoid robotics as android martial artists landed knockout roundhouse kicks and robot teams marched into the arena heralded by flag-waving captains astride giant robotic dogs. The games’ blue-riband event, the 100m, did not disappoint when the robot-sprinters ran quicker than Usain Bolt before slamming mindlessly into a padded wall in a blaze of sparks, flames and flying mechanical limbs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hilarity, unease and relief: games show China is not over the finish line in humanoid robot race

articles.author: Peter Walker and Charlotte Edwardes
articles.description:
Former PM believes Northern Ireland will leave UK in the long term – but remains opposed to Scottish independence
The former prime minister Gordon Brown has said it is inevitable that Ireland will become united at some point in the future, in a wide-ranging interview with the Guardian.
While he added that any union would necessarily be “a long process” and based on mutual agreement, Brown’s comments are notable both because of his vehement opposition to Scottish independence, but also because of his involvement in government in efforts to bring peace to Northern Ireland.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ireland will be united, says Gordon Brown

articles.author: Kim Willsher
articles.description:
Architect of Srebrenica genocide is dead but those scarred by his atrocities say his ideology is still shockingly pervasive
To most of the world, he was and will always be the “Butcher of Bosnia”, a grim epithet but one that still fails to fully convey the evil and horror inflicted on its people by Gen Ratko Mladić, who died in prison on Thursday.
As commander of the Bosnian Serb forces, Mladić was responsible for the killing of an estimated 100,000 men, women and children during the savage breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s. He was most notoriously the architect of ethnic cleansing and the genocide at Srebrenica in which at least 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were slaughtered.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘The butcher may be gone, but to many he is a hero’: victims condemn glorification of Mladić

articles.author: Ima Caldwell
articles.description:
More than 40 Australians are among several thousand people unaccounted for after catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border

How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An 11-year-old child, an ADF member and many other pilgrims and trekkers have been named among the Australians missing after deadly flash floods and landslides tore through valleys on the Nepal-Tibet border.
As of Saturday there were 41 Australians among almost 2,500 people reported missing in the disaster, including at least 777 foreigners. At least 93,000 people were estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What we know about the Australians missing in the Nepal floods

articles.author: Wendy Frew ; Lucy Campbell, Keely Aouga, Nadeem Badshah, Tom Ambrose, Mabel Banfield-Nwachi, Taz Ali and Adam Fulton
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed

‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?

More now on the Nepali army’s rescue operation to save about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by Wednesday’s flooding.
“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.
The army is still working to safely evacuate more than 100 people trapped in the same tunnel.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Search continues as number missing in Nepal-Tibet floods rises to 2,478 – as it happened

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell, Keely Aouga and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Trump arch will alter sightlines of many Washington DC landmarks, report says

Sign up for the US Breaking News email

A reminder that we are covering the latest out of Jackson Hole, Wyoming, where Kevin Warsh – the new chair of the Federal Reserve – will deliver his first speech as the head of the US central bank at the annual economic policy symposium.
As my colleagues note, Warsh is under pressure to provide clarity on how the Federal Reserve should handle with inflation if price pressures don’t abate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: National Park Service supports Trump’s arch even though it would have ‘adverse effects’ on other DC monuments, report says – as it happened

articles.author: Petra Stock
articles.description:
The $134,000 cost of the statue of the former Victorian premier has been heavily criticised by the Liberal opposition

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Carroll government in Victoria has cancelled controversial plans for a statue of former Labor premier Daniel Andrews.
Work began in May on the statue commemorating the former premier’s more than 3,000 days in office, as part of a 1999 policy recognising long-serving Victorian premiers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Controversial plans for a Daniel Andrews sculpture officially scrapped by Victorian government

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves
Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves.
The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Six more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near Steyning
A 41-year-old man has died and at least six other people have been injured after a large sign fell at a Christian festival in West Sussex, police said.
The man, from Eastbourne, East Sussex, was pronounced dead at the scene after the incident at the Big Church festival near Steyning on Friday afternoon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Man, 41, dies after large sign falls at Christian festival in West Sussex

articles.author: Stephanie Convery and Cait Kelly in Kathmandu
articles.description:
There are now 41 Australians missing, and four rapid response team members are expected to arrive in Kathmandu

At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods

How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The number of Australians who were reported missing in the catastrophic Nepal flooding disaster has risen to 41, as one family celebrates after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.
It means three additional Australians were confirmed missing overnight – up from 38 who remained unaccounted for on Friday evening.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Number of Australians missing in Nepal’s deadly floods rises again, as Albanese deploys more personnel

articles.author: Gabrielle Canon
articles.description:
Nearly 600 days after the devastating 2025 fires, thousands of Los Angeles residents are still waiting for more than $15bn in federal funds to rebuild their communities 
As thousands of residents in Spokane, Washington, begin to grapple with a long recovery after a destructive set of blazes that consumed hundreds of homes in the state’s second most populated city this month, victims of the Los Angeles firestorm broke a grim record – they have faced the longest delay in modern history for federal aid.
Nearly 600 days since a historic firestorm roared into communities across Los Angeles, reducing more than 16,000 structures to ash and toxic debris, the Trump administration has failed to appropriate more than $15bn in long-term recovery funds that are crucial to rebuilding. The delay in supplying the badly needed funds is months longer than the last record set when victims of the Maui fires had to wait 500 days to receive the support, LAist noted this week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Los Angeles fire survivors face record wait for federal disaster aid under Trump

articles.author: Press Association
articles.description:
Cleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officers
Seven more men have been arrested as part of an operation tackling alleged organised crime after the head-on crash on the A66 that resulted in seven deaths, Cleveland police have said.
Officers said four men, aged 21, 25, 35 and 40, were being held on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after a vehicle crashed into a house in Steele Crescent, Middlesbrough.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police arrest seven more men in aftermath of deadly A66 crash

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
National Park Service, which backs the 250ft arch, says it is likely to disrupt historical significance of dozens of sites
A new National Park Service report backs Donald Trump’s proposed arch, despite what it says are adverse effects to the sightlines of a host of landmarks in Washington, including the Washington Monument and the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials.
The report released on Friday says the 250ft-tall (76-meter) memorial arch is likely to disrupt the historical significance of dozens of sites near its planned location adjacent to the Arlington Memorial Bridge.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump arch will alter sightlines of many Washington DC landmarks, report says

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
Climber, stuck on 6in ridge, had veered off treacherous path and ‘any fall would almost certainly be fatal’
An ill-fated move left a man stranded on a 6in ledge over 10,000ft off the ground for hours in California’s Sierra Nevada mountain range, before a volunteer rescue team came to his aid.
The climber, who has not been publicly identified, had been scaling the Mendenhall couloir, a gully on the face of Laurel mountain, with a friend on Saturday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Volunteers rescue man stuck on 10,000ft-high ledge in Sierra Nevada

articles.author: Tom Phillips Latin America correspondent
articles.description:
Critics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves  ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’
Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.
Several media outlets this week reported that the Trump administration – which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Venezuelan opposition up in arms over reports US wants big stake in oil and gas

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty level
Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit, western officials have said.
While Russia is still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the last two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Bidur, Sam Jones and agencies
articles.description:
Federation says it fears death toll of nearly 600 will continue to rise as rescuers reach cut-off areas

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?

The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, which have killed nearly 600 people, left another 1,900 missing, and triggered a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross

articles.author: Jon Henley Europe correspondent
articles.description:
Norwegians gather to remember monarch whose death comes amid scandal over links between crown princess and Jeffrey Epstein
Norwegians have gathered in their thousands to pay their respects to King Harald V, Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, who has died, aged 89, in Oslo. He was succeeded immediately by his son, King Haakon VIII.
The new king thanked “the government and Norwegian people for their support and sympathy for the royal family at this time”. A period of national mourning was announced as crowds left wreaths and messages outside the royal palace in Oslo.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Norway’s King Harald dies aged 89

articles.author: Rachel Hall and Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Desperate relatives trying to reach loved ones last seen in area where entire villages have been swept away

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?

Families are rushing to Nepal to search for the 33 British nationals who are still missing, as fears mount over the risk of a second wave of flooding in the region.
The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 538 people, while more than 1,500 remain missing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Families of 33 missing Britons rush to Nepal as fears grow of more floods

articles.author: Anna Betts
articles.description:
Remnants from tropical storm could cause heavy rainfall on Leeward Islands and affect Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola
Remnants of Tropical Storm Dolly, which has been downgraded to an “open tropical wave”, were moving still across the Atlantic Ocean toward the Leeward Islands, and could bring heavy rainfall to parts of the Caribbean this weekend, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Friday..
Dolly, which formed on Thursday, had maximum sustained winds of near 40mph (65km/h) with higher gusts on Friday morning. Later on Friday, forecasters said that Dolly was no longer a Tropical Storm, and had “become an open tropical wave”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tropical Storm Dolly downgraded to ‘open tropical wave’ as it heads to Caribbean

articles.author: Deborah Cole in Berlin
articles.description:
Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours
Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.
Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid

articles.author: Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent
articles.description:
Scale of devastation emerges in Nepal as reporters reach disaster area, but Chinese state media focus more on rescue efforts

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

In the days since an enormous glacier in the Himalayas snapped away from a mountaintop and cascaded into the valley below, the true scale of the devastation caused by the flash floods in Nepal and Tibet is still unfolding.
But the picture is emerging far more quickly in Nepal than in China, where strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Chinese control of information hampers assessment of Tibet flood damage

articles.author: Anna Betts
articles.description:
Thai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboard
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop in Thailand next week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spending more than 250 consecutive days at sea supporting US operations against Iran amid recent reports of poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.
The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by the USS George Washington, and is now heading home to San Diego. A Thai navy official told Reuters this week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea

articles.author: Tom Perkins in Detroit
articles.description:
Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races
Every day $1bn worth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry.
News this week of Donald Trump’s escalating trade spat with Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Bidur, Sam Jones and agencies
articles.description:
Risk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surge

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

Tell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?

Rescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding.
Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal and China said that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lake

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu, Sam Jones and Amy Hawkins
articles.description:
Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away 

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

What caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?

The international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet on Thursday as authorities warned that a lake ⁠formed at the ⁠site ⁠where the ​deadly torrents occurred ⁠was rising and ⁠at risk ​of ‌bursting.
The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 469 people and left more than 1,300 missing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burst

articles.author: Jordyn Beazley
articles.description:
Book was removed for review earlier this month following complaint but reinstated after petition and State Library letter to Waverley council

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Sydney library has returned to its borrowing shelves a book critical of Israel called How to Sell a Genocide following a public campaign and an intervention from the State Library of New South Wales.
Waverley library removed the book “for review” earlier this month after the Jewish news outlet JWire reported it had approached the council.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bondi library returns book How to Sell a Genocide to shelves after State Library ‘outlines the law’

articles.author: Aisha Down
articles.description:
Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands
In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.
For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?

articles.author: Adam Fulton, Nadeem Badshah, Lucy Campbell, Shannon Ho, Tom Ambrose, Mabel Banfield-Nwachi and Martin Belam
articles.description:
This live blog has now closed – but our coverage continues at a new blog here
Eyewitness accounts have been emerging from the Tibetan side of the border, with a woman saying she was travelling from Gyirong town towards Nepal on Wednesday morning when her group encountered the flood about 4km from Gyirong port.
“Trees and electricity poles had already been knocked down, and the flood water was bearing down on us. We didn’t dare turn around, so we could only reverse,” the woman, surnamed Fang, told Xiaoxiang Morning News.
I was really scared. My whole body was trembling.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Warning of fresh danger from rising lake water in Nepal – as it happened

articles.author: George Chidi
articles.description:
Mark Carney rejects attempt to rename lake as did several US governors, with Tony Evers mocking the move

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday directing the federal government to rename Lake Ontario, making it Lake America, amid his escalating trade war with Canada.
The order directs federal agencies to adopt the name-change on US maps, documents and databases. But Trump has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake, nor to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America

articles.author: Jonathan Watts
articles.description:
Unusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastrophe

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

What caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?

The devastating flash flood that has ripped through the border communities of Nepal and Tibet has heightened fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions, threatening millions of people.
Satellite imagery suggests a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the deadly torrent of mud, water and ice that tore along the Bhotekoshi River on Wednesday. It swept away buildings and roads and left at least 360 dead and 1,400 missing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Climate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warn

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime
The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.
Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’

articles.author: Robert Tait in Washington
articles.description:
President denies visit was to gain support for Iran sanctions or due to fears that Putin plans to ‘test Nato resolve’
Donald Trump has downplayed a visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, as “semi-routine” after he turned up in the Russian capital unannounced, triggering a wave of speculation about the reasons for his trip.
Ratcliffe was reported to have flown to Moscow on a government transport plane on Tuesday in a rare visit after taking off from the Andrews air force base in Maryland.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump downplays Moscow visit by CIA director as ‘semi-routine’

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking
South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.
A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs

articles.author: Kat Lay Global health correspondent
articles.description:
The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected
A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?
Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?

articles.author: Seham Tantesh in Gaza, and Julian Borger
articles.description:
Efforts to rebuild domestic food production face severe challenges and have come at deadly cost
As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive.
With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive

articles.author: Deepa Parent
articles.description:
As photojournalist sentenced to 15 years, rights groups warn law would turn civic engagement into security crime
Iran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign media, in a move human rights groups have said attempts to “sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world”.
For journalists, researchers and even ordinary citizens, the proposed law being discussed by Iranian lawmakers this month could make speaking to international audiences and groups a potential criminal act and restrict coverage of events such as January’s mass anti-regime protests.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran seeks to criminalise all contact with foreign media in ‘chilling’ crackdown

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Internal calls to end war get louder as Gulf neighbours plan alternative pipelines to cut reliance on waterway
Is the strait of Hormuz, recently cited by the office of the Iranian supreme leader as “the pillar of Iran’s new security order”, and as transformative as possessing a nuclear weapon, in reality becoming a fast-diminishing asset, leaving Iran increasingly vulnerable to the new planned US wave of economic sanctions?
It is the key debate that is raging inside Iran, with many different conclusions being drawn for Tehran’s negotiating strategy. Those who warn the strait’s value as a chokehold on the world economy will erode, leaving the country without foreign exchange reserves, argue that Iran’s negotiators should seek a deal soon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran faces strait of Hormuz paradox as strategic value of chokehold erodes

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell, Keely Aouga and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Trump arch will alter sightlines of many Washington DC landmarks, report says

Sign up for the US Breaking News email

A reminder that we are covering the latest out of Jackson Hole, Wyoming, where Kevin Warsh – the new chair of the Federal Reserve – will deliver his first speech as the head of the US central bank at the annual economic policy symposium.
As my colleagues note, Warsh is under pressure to provide clarity on how the Federal Reserve should handle with inflation if price pressures don’t abate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: National Park Service supports Trump’s arch even though it would have ‘adverse effects’ on other DC monuments, report says – as it happened

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves
Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves.
The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
National Park Service, which backs the 250ft arch, says it is likely to disrupt historical significance of dozens of sites
A new National Park Service report backs Donald Trump’s proposed arch, despite what it says are adverse effects to the sightlines of a host of landmarks in Washington, including the Washington Monument and the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials.
The report released on Friday says the 250ft-tall (76-meter) memorial arch is likely to disrupt the historical significance of dozens of sites near its planned location adjacent to the Arlington Memorial Bridge.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump arch will alter sightlines of many Washington DC landmarks, report says

articles.author: Gaya Gupta
articles.description:
However, Kevin Warsh didn’t say if interest rates would change in coming months, as inflation remains stubborn
The US Federal Reserve is not done fighting high inflation, its chair, Kevin Warsh, said in his first major speech in the role on Friday, emphasizing that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”.
Warsh did not indicate where the Fed will take interest rates in the coming months, despite US inflation remaining stubbornly above the central bank’s 2% target amid the war in Iran. But his speech was taken by markets as a signal that rates may rise in the coming months, a move that may put him at odds with Donald Trump, who has aggressively called for rates to be cut.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fed chair says delivering ‘stable prices’ is central bank’s job as inflation persists

articles.author: Shrai Popat in Washington
articles.description:
President faces criticism over plan to import up to 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef without charging higher tariffs
Donald Trump has pledged to allow cattle ranchers and farmers to process their own food amid a backlash from the US agricultural sector over his decision to pause US tariffs on foreign beef.
The US president has been sharply criticized, including from members of his own party, since announcing the US will temporarily import up to 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef without charging higher tariffs in an effort to bring down prices.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump pledges to allow cattle ranchers to process own food amid beef imports backlash

articles.author: Robert Reich
articles.description:
Terrified of being seen as a loser, Donald Trump is nonsensically lashing out – even against our old friend Canada
I’m still grieving Dolly Parton. I never met her and always wanted to. She was almost exactly my age and my height and had values I deeply admired. Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.
Which brings me to the person whose values are as far from Dolly Parton’s as any human could possibly be and still claim to be human. I’m referring, of course, to the current occupant of the Oval Office.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Dolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying president | Robert Reich

articles.author: Presented by Jonathan Freedland with Dan Alexander, produced by Nada Smiljanic and Danielle Stephens
articles.description:
Jonathan Freedland speaks to Dan Alexander of Forbes about how Donald Trump made so much money last year at the same time trade wars, military wars and a rising national debt hurt the US economy
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How did Trump get so rich? | Politics Weekly America

articles.author: Sidney Blumenthal
articles.description:
The president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotion
Donald Trump has framed his theme for the midterm elections. It has come to him as naturally and inevitably as staring into the mirror, beyond any logic or argument, his definitive answer to no specific issue, providing no understanding of any particular problem, but transcending all of them. His political theme is more primal than programmatic, more instinctive than analytical, a heartfelt expression to protect his greatest romantic attachment, his obsessive fixation, his idealized object: himself.
Trump’s campaign theme is unrequited love. Unlike the pollsters, media consultants and pundits, he alone has grasped the magnitude and the source of the existential crisis threatening his politics. He has identified the problem for the Republicans as the faltering measure of complete devotion to him. His demand has nothing to do with mutual affection. It is a ploy to reassert his slipping control, a manipulative test to prove loyalty to him, or else. There can be no absolute rule without an absolute ruler; no absolute ruler without absolute submission; no absolute submission without the expression of absolute love. His sadness at its fading gives way to anger, paranoia and greater acts of retribution. He equates the fear he instills as a form of love. Trump accepts subservience, from whatever motive, as affection or its closest equivalent. He cares nothing about sincerity, so it’s all in the show. The less love displayed, the more fear required. Yet there is no rebound, but only deeper rejection.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited love | Sidney Blumenthal

articles.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
articles.description:
Scott Jennings has pivoted from his early critiques and caught the White House’s eye with pro-Trump commentary on CNN
In 2016, a month before the presidential election that Donald Trump would win, the longtime Republican strategist Scott Jennings described him as “a vulgar, crude, braggadocious, desperate-to-impress playboy who tends to view most everything through a sexual lens”.
After Trump’s loss in the 2020 election, Jennings excoriated Trump’s conduct during the January 6 Capitol insurrection, saying he “clearly violated his oath of office to preserve, protect and defend the constitution to the best of [his] ability”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A conservative strategist called for ‘getting rid of Trump’ three years ago. Could he be his next press secretary?

articles.author: Margaret Sullivan
articles.description:
The singer had a serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity. We could all stand to channel it a bit more
The moment that the world found out that Dolly Parton had died, I was in a hair salon in the reddest congressional district in New York state. The neighborhood on the shore of Lake Erie where I move every summer voted solidly for Donald Trump in 2024.
I often pass a lawn sign that has something misogynistic to say about New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul, and the mere mention of Kamala Harris’s name can bring derisive jokes. Of course, there certainly are liberals and independents to be found, but on balance the area leans right.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Dolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her? | Margaret Sullivan

articles.author: Dustin Guastella and Erica Etelson
articles.description:
It’s about ‘kitchen-table populism’: focusing on Americans’ day-to-day economic struggles
This year’s Democratic primaries look and sound a lot more populist than usual. Brian Poindexter, a union iron worker running on a “workers first” message, won a House primary outside Cleveland. Sherrod Brown is mounting a Senate comeback in Ohio on the same “rigged system” message that has allowed him to outshine other Democrats in Ohio. Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger who built his career fighting corporate landowners, is the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine. And Josh Turek, a self-described “prairie populist”, is on the Senate ballot in Iowa.
In fact, according to research we’ve conducted through the Center for Working-Class Politics (CWCP), more than 70% of 2026 Democratic candidates now rely on populist rhetoric in their campaigns, laying the blame for our broken system on rich elites of one kind or another.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: We surveyed 6,000 Americans. Here is the winning message for Democrats | Dustin Guastella

articles.author: David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
In his new book, congressman Jared Huffman argues that theocratic insurgency has only grown more powerful after Donald Trump returned to the White House
Crosses, shofars and “Appeal to Heaven” flags. Rioters praying with their hands aloft as police officers are brutalised. January 6 2021 is widely remembered as a deadly insurrection by supporters of Donald Trump; but for Congressman Jared Huffman, who was locked down alone in his office that day, something else stands out.
It was a very Christian coup.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘A Bible-sized blind spot’: congressman sounds alarm on rising Christian nationalism

articles.author: Chris Stein
articles.description:
Adam Hamilton, a liberal megachurch pastor, is challenging incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall in this year’s midterm election
In one of the first ads of his campaign to represent Kansas in the US Senate, the Democrat Adam Hamilton stands grilling steaks at a barbecue and attacks his opponent, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, for supporting “tariffs and war”.
If history is any guide, it is Hamilton who is set to get cooked. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close. But he and his supporters believe circumstances have conspired to end this streak – and potentially deliver Democrats control of the Senate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932. Will that change in November?

articles.author: Roque Planas in Comstock, Texas
articles.description:
The president’s border wall plan could damage or destroy ‘the oldest-known books in North America’
On an overcast summer morning, Carolyn Boyd, an archeologist at Texas State University, stood at the foot of a cave in west Texas, looking up toward a series of towering murals painted on a rock wall. Three massive human-like figures soared toward an overhang that had sheltered the painting from the elements since they were drawn here perhaps 4,000 years ago.
An artist herself, Boyd knows how hard it would have been to paint these long, crisp lines. Before starting, the bands of Indigenous hunter-gatherers who lived in this west Texas valley, where the Pecos River empties into the Rio Grande, would have spent weeks pulverizing gypsum, hematite, limonite and manganese to make paint. They would have gathered massive quantities of sotol stalks to fold its fibers into scaffolding. The painting itself would have required teamwork and precision, with people at the bottom guiding artists on the wall as they painted figures stretching up to 30ft tall.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s border wall construction threatens rock art as old as the pyramids: ‘The ancestors are still here’

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Paul Owen ; produced by Bryony Moore ; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
articles.description:
One of Donald Trump’s closest and most devoted aides, Natalie Harp, has faced intense media scrutiny this week, after a Democratic senator, Jon Ossoff, name-checked her in a speech that went viral. So what do we know about Harp, who is often referred to as the ‘human printer’? And why is everybody talking about her relationship with Trump? Helen Pidd speaks to international news editor Paul Owen
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why is Trump’s ‘human printer’ aide Natalie Harp suddenly in the spotlight? - The Latest

articles.author: Jonathan Freedland with Jill Lepore . Produced by Nada Smiljanic, and Danielle Stephens
articles.description:
Less than three months to go until the midterms, voters are thinking about grocery prices, the Iran war and… datacentres.

This week, Jonathan Freedland speaks to historian Jill Lepore about how this latest AI backlash could influence those all-important elections in November. Are we seeing the beginning of the end of the 'artificial state'?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Historian Jill Lepore on the datacentre backlash | Politics Weekly America

articles.description:
The US president waxed lyrical about grass being added around the new White House helipad in front of the media. 'You know, grass has a life like humans have a life,' Trump said
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump talks about grass as he shows off White House renovations – video

articles.author: Rupert Jones
articles.description:
Moving tariffs will cushion the blow from the October price cap rise and the increase widely predicted for January
With higher energy bills looming and warnings of worse to come in the new year, many households could save up to £173 a year by switching to a fixed deal.
Millions of households in Great Britain will face the highest energy charges in three years after it was announced that the government’s price cap will rise again in October. This will be the second increase in three months.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Households could save up to £173 a year by switching to fixed energy deal

articles.author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
articles.description:
Exclusive: Number of times AI lies, ignores instructions and pursues goals in harmful ways almost doubles in July
Incidents of AIs escaping users’ control to lie, ignore instructions and pursue goals in harmful ways have hit a new high, according to research that also suggests the severity of deception and misalignment is worsening.
Analysis of real-world loss of control incidents involving AI models flagged by businesses and individuals almost doubled in July compared with June, with more than 300 cases in the month, according to the Loss of Control Observatory, which monitors reports made by AI users on the social media platform X.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sharp rise in incidents of AI escaping users’ control, research finds

articles.author: Mark Sweney
articles.description:
Planning delays and slow 5G upgrades could leave the UK unable to cope with a surge in AI-related traffic 
The UK risks becoming a laggard in the global AI race as crucial telecoms upgrades to harness the technology fall behind rival nations, according to senior industry executives.
The infrastructure AI race has centred on the need to build datacentres, and to ensure they have access to the huge water and energy supplies required to cool and supply the computational power to train and run AI models.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK risks falling behind in AI race without faster telecoms upgrades, say executives

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose
articles.description:
As one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatility
Europe is on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years, which has triggered “winter panic” among energy traders, experts have warned.
The EU’s gas stocks were 63% full in the last week of August, well below the 80% average for late August over recent years and among the lowest levels ever recorded for this time of year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years

articles.author: Peter Walker and Charlotte Edwardes
articles.description:
Former PM believes Northern Ireland will leave UK in the long term – but remains opposed to Scottish independence
The former prime minister Gordon Brown has said it is inevitable that Ireland will become united at some point in the future, in a wide-ranging interview with the Guardian.
While he added that any union would necessarily be “a long process” and based on mutual agreement, Brown’s comments are notable both because of his vehement opposition to Scottish independence, but also because of his involvement in government in efforts to bring peace to Northern Ireland.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ireland will be united, says Gordon Brown

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Six more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near Steyning
A 41-year-old man has died and at least six other people have been injured after a large sign fell at a Christian festival in West Sussex, police said.
The man, from Eastbourne, East Sussex, was pronounced dead at the scene after the incident at the Big Church festival near Steyning on Friday afternoon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Man, 41, dies after large sign falls at Christian festival in West Sussex

articles.author: Press Association
articles.description:
Cleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officers
Seven more men have been arrested as part of an operation tackling alleged organised crime after the head-on crash on the A66 that resulted in seven deaths, Cleveland police have said.
Officers said four men, aged 21, 25, 35 and 40, were being held on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after a vehicle crashed into a house in Steele Crescent, Middlesbrough.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police arrest seven more men in aftermath of deadly A66 crash

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah and agencies
articles.description:
About 125 firefighters tackle blaze at Neasden waste facility as nearby Amazon warehouse is evacuated
A large fire broke out at a waste facility close to Wembley Stadium in north-west London, disrupting tube and train lines in the area.
Twenty fire engines and about 125 firefighters were sent to tackle the blaze at a mixed-waste facility on an industrial estate in Neasden, less than a mile from the venue.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Large fire near Wembley Stadium disrupts tube and rail services

articles.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
articles.description:
High court quashes latest restriction on Orange Order march, reigniting political row over Garvaghy Road
The boiling cauldron known as Drumcree that used to scald and torment Northern Ireland each summer gradually cooled two decades ago, leaving it as a name for the history books.
Instead of pitched battles between Orangemen and police around the parish church near Portadown in County Armagh, and the murderous sectarian violence they triggered across the region, gave way to a de facto truce.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Drumcree ruling raises fears of sectarian confrontation in Northern Ireland

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor in Munich
articles.description:
Leading cardiovascular health groups reclassify overlooked causes and introduce sex-specific diagnostic thresholds
Doctors have agreed the world’s first universal definition of a heart attack, paving the way for millions of women to finally receive better treatment after decades of being “deprioritised”.
In one of the biggest procedural shake-ups in a generation, the world’s four leading cardiovascular health groups have signed off on new guidance for healthcare professionals when seeing suspected heart attack patients.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New heart attack definition promises better care for women

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Campaigners say ‘seismic shift’ follows years of pressure to sever ties with oil and gas firm
The London Science Museum has ended its decades-long partnership with the oil and gas company BP in what has been described as a “seismic shift” for the museum.
The Science Museum Group academy, which was established in 2018 to provide training and resources, announced on Friday that it would be ending its partnership with BP. In a statement, the director and chief executive of the Science Museum Group, Sir Ian Blatchford, said the partnership had “drawn to a close at the end of the current contract term”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: London Science Museum cuts links with BP after decades of partnership

articles.author: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent
articles.description:
Experts say imported eggs served in cafes and restaurants may be behind hundreds of infections and one death
Salmonella cases in the UK are expected to rise until the common source is identified, something that is notoriously difficult to establish, experts have warned.
There have been 474 confirmed cases and one death linked to the current outbreak, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), with the latest investigations suggesting it is associated with eating imported eggs in cafes and restaurants.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Salmonella cases in UK likely to rise until source of outbreak is found

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.description:
Readers react to an article by Emine Saner about the arrival of US-style tipping culture in British restaurants and bars
Articles comparing tipping culture in the UK to that in the US (‘It’s absolutely criminal’: US tipping culture has reached the UK – and is causing chaos, 24 August) do not go into the complication of minimum wage calculation in the US. There, wait staff are paid a low base rate, but employers must ensure their earnings are topped up to at least the minimum wage through tips.
As an American who has lived in the UK for 27 years, I have endless discussions with American visiting friends about tipping, and how their example of cultural imperialism has resulted in the distortion of worker value for some of the reasons set out in this article (for example, more attractive people get better tips). The assumption is that people who wait on others don’t have as much money as the tipper, but do we know if this is true? With this logic, should we tip the person who serves us at TK Maxx or Aldi?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fair pay, service charges and the pressure to tip | Letters

articles.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
articles.description:
Brazil has failed to prove compliance with EU rules on use of antibiotics in cattle and poultry farming
The UK’s leading farming organisations and animal health experts have called for an urgent ban on imports of Brazilian meat, in light of concerns over the safety of imports.
The National Farmers’ Union in England and its sister organisations in the devolved administrations wrote to the government on Friday warning that public health was at risk.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK urged to ban imports of Brazilian meat over health concerns

articles.author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
articles.description:
Government says Green leader’s proposed moratorium on ‘energy-guzzling’ AI projects would be disaster for economy
Labour has rejected calls to pause construction of major AI infrastructure in Britain after the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was time to “slam the brakes on these energy-guzzling, water-guzzling datacentres”.
The government hit back at the opposition party’s proposal of a “moratorium other than [for] local-scale datacentres for the local community”, saying it “would be a disaster for jobs and national security”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Labour rejects Zack Polanski’s call to ‘slam brakes’ on building AI datacentres

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: PM also warns his ministers against trying to influence vote when bill returns to Commons next month
Andy Burnham has told Labour MPs that he will not cast a vote when the assisted dying bill returns to the Commons next month, to avoid influencing the debate.
While supporters of the measure welcomed his move, No 10 officials said the prime minister had no wish to affect the process in either direction, and was just doing what he thought was best to allow MPs to reach their own collective view.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Andy Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying bill to avoid swaying debate

articles.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
articles.description:
Speech part of effort to strengthen National Rally party’s international ties before Marine Le Pen’s presidential bid
The French far-right leader Jordan Bardella is to give a speech at Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham next week as he attempts to boost international ties before Marine Le Pen’s bid for the French presidency next spring.
Le Pen’s far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN) is high in the polls and she is predicted to reach the final round of the French presidential race in May.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: French far-right leader Jordan Bardella to address Reform UK party conference

articles.author: Sarah Butler
articles.description:
Chair Allan Leighton says lower prices and an improved online service are attracting more shoppers
Asda has heralded its first trading growth in more than two years as the supermarket’s boss said it was attracting more shoppers with lower prices and an improved online service.
Allan Leighton, the executive chair of the UK’s third-largest grocer, said a 0.2% rise in sales at established stores, excluding fuel, in the seven weeks to 18 August was “a huge milestone” that was “psychologically important for the business”. In the preceding three months, sales had fallen 2.3%.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Asda returns to growth after more than two years

articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor
articles.description:
Christian Drogan’s Invading Britain shows former builder turned journalist trying to travel from France to England in small boat
Rupert Murdoch’s online channel TalkTV is facing criticism after it did not disclose that a journalist who travelled to Britain in a small boat for a documentary was a Reform party member and activist.
The channel revealed the “world exclusive” this week, stating that the treacherous journey had made the former builder turned journalist Christian Drogan the first British man “to invade his own country”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: TalkTV under fire for not disclosing reporter’s ties to Reform UK in Channel crossing film

articles.author: Lauren Almeida
articles.description:
Average cost of petrol reaches 161.6p a litre, while diesel costs average of 183.4p, according to the AA
UK petrol prices have hit their highest level since 2022, piling more financial pressure on motorists before the bank holiday weekend.
The average cost of petrol has reached 161.6p a litre, while diesel costs an average of 183.4p a litre, according to the AA breakdown company.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK petrol prices hit highest level in almost four years as bank holiday getaway looms

articles.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
articles.description:
As well as being quieter, cheaper to run and easier to clean, induction cookers can cut kitchen temperatures by up to 10C
Leaping flames, searing heat, copious sweat and scorchingly inventive swearing – restaurant kitchens are never a place for the faint-hearted, but this summer they have been sweltering in successive heatwaves to a dangerous degree.
Some restaurants, cafes and bakeries in the UK grew so hot that they were forced to close, or reduce their hours, for the safety of their staff. There is still no maximum working temperature, despite calls from the TUC, and tens of thousands of kitchen staff are thought to have carried on working in “furnace-like” conditions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The chefs turning down the heat by switching from gas to electric

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Hundreds of foreigners were in area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages when disaster struck

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.
Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Which countries have citizens killed or missing after Nepal-Tibet flash flood?

articles.author: Heather Stewart and Lauren Almeida
articles.description:
Roadmap for increasing department’s share of GDP will be deferred until next year’s review
The chancellor will delay setting out when the UK will meet the target of allocating 3% of GDP on defence until next year’s spending review, the Treasury has confirmed.
John Healey resigned as defence secretary in June under Keir Starmer’s leadership, accusing the prime minister of being “unable” and the Treasury “unwilling” to “commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Healey’s budget to duck setting a date for 3% defence spending target

articles.author: Jamie Grierson
articles.description:
Soaring demand for services has led to tenfold increase in spending in a year in some areas, says NHS Alliance
NHS leaders have warned that the costs of meeting soaring demand for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism services in England are “running out of control” and have become unsustainable, with spending in some areas rising by as much as tenfold over the course of a year.
The NHS Alliance, which represents health managers, said the rise in demand since the coronavirus pandemic was forcing some to close waiting lists and look at reining in other services they provide.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ADHD and autism costs in England ‘running out of control’, NHS leaders warn

articles.author: Jamie Grierson
articles.description:
About 80 people sign open letter to Andy Burnham calling for legislation to protect voice ownership
Nicola Coughlan, Hugh Bonneville and Matt Lucas are among a group of actors backing a campaign against artificial intelligence voice cloning.
Save Our Voices Now, which is also being supported by Luke Evans, Jen Brister, Siobhán McSweeney and Pearl Mackie, aims to stop the practice in which AI technology is used to replicate a real person’s voice to say anything it is prompted to.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nicola Coughlan and Matt Lucas among stars backing campaign against AI voice cloning

articles.author: Natalie Wint and Alex Daniel
articles.description:
Problems including derailments have hit network during one of the hottest and driest summers on record 
Britain’s railways have faced a string of heat-related problems this summer, including a derailment near Lewes in East Sussex two weeks ago that injured 30 people, and another the next day when the rear carriages of a Greater Anglia train derailed “in an upright position” at Wickford railway station in Essex, with no reported injuries.
The problems came during one of the hottest and driest summers on record, with a series of heatwaves, and drought declared across large parts of England and Wales. Britain’s railways, built for a cooler, wetter climate, have been put under pressure. Network Rail said the summer had “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Britain’s railways are struggling in the heat – and can they be fixed?

articles.author: Steven Morris
articles.description:
A zero-emission compact hydrogen power plant will drive the two stages at Clifton Down in Bristol
When Lorde, Little Simz and Wet Leg stride on to stages in Bristol this weekend, they will not only be entertaining tens of thousands of festivalgoers but taking part in what is being billed as a world-first clean power project.

articles.description:
Before The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’
The game that graced us with Bathtub Geralt, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, arrived more than a decade ago. So it was a touch surprising this summer when developers CD Projekt Red announced a new expansion to the venerable adventure, titled Songs of the Past, for next year. It will release alongside a full remaster of the original game, which will be free for anyone who bought it back in 2015. (The studio is also working on a sequel, The Witcher 4, but that’s not due until 2028.)
As it turns out, this is all possible thanks to a partnership with Fool’s Theory, a studio founded by CD Projekt Red veterans, which took on the brunt of the development work. “We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years,” explains Marcin Blacha, VP story director at CD Projekt Red. “Of course, we moved on to Cyberpunk 2077 and now The Witcher 4, as well as our other projects. But because we knew The Witcher 4 would take time, we saw a gap in our release calendar where Songs of the Past could go. Thankfully, we were able to find the right partner to help execute it.”

articles.description:

We’re all escaping something when we play video games. Mostly it’s the drabness of real life, where we don’t get to command kingdoms using armies of dragons, win Champions League trophies with our local team, or inhabit the body of an improbably speedy hedgehog.
Sometimes I play them because I want to escape from the version of me that gets paralysed by depression, and boy has the black dog been sniffing at my bits recently, because the Atlantic Ocean is separating me from my wife for a few months. For 30 years she has been the light that banishes that darkness, and I am honestly lost without her. If that sounds pathetic, you haven’t met her. She leaves everybody she meets feeling better. It’s a superpower that warrants a call from the X-Men.

articles.description:
This week’s settlement without liability was pragmatic, but it doesn’t change the inevitability of further lawsuits around the world 
Not many people would count paying $18bn they didn’t expect to when they woke up that morning as a victory. Yet for Meta, the owners of Facebook and Instagram, the agreement with 52 US attorneys general to settle claims that it designed its products to be addictive to children, and misled people about their safety, could be described as a win of sorts.
Meta denies wrongdoing, and the amount it plans to pay will be spread over a decade. Some of it is contingent on other big tech firms not named in its case coughing up too. The cash is chump change for Meta, which made around $60bn in profit last year. More damaging to the tech giant in the long run could be the agreement to unwind some of the mechanics it has spent two decades perfecting to keep us on its platforms.

articles.author: Lewis Gordon
articles.description:
PlayStation 5, Xbox Series S/X, PC; Asobo Studio
The medieval franchise is transplanted to Crete, conjuring action-adventure magic from familiar ingredients

The path in Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a familiar one. Amid ancient ruins and sun-dappled gorges, a young woman, Sophia, dutifully treads the same footsteps as a Minoan warrior from millennia ago, one with whom she seems to share a visionary connection. The “resonance” between these two characters is made clear by their echoing actions – a crank pushed in the bronze age that still works in the medieval present, for example. Through these spliced timelines, it becomes clear that Sophia, compelled by her supernatural gift, possesses little agency. Destiny beckons her forwards.
This is a smart meta concept for a game that, at its most basic level, boils down to keeping your left thumb planted firmly on the analogue stick, always pushing Sophia onwards in linear fashion. You jostle her through ornate corridors rendered as higgledy-piggledy pirate camps and cobbled Venetian streets. For the greater part of the game, you propel her through the Minoan remains of Crete, which harbour a dark and terrible secret. It is classic third-person action-adventure fare, building on the template laid down by the likes of Tomb Raider and then refined and complicated by titles such as The Last of Us. Little, from an interactive perspective, surprises: you dash, vault and swing between teetering podiums, squeeze through tiny gaps in rock and crouch behind conveniently placed walls to avoid enemies.

The flat routines of a dead end railway job screen out an approaching menace in a quietly intriguing game from the indie developer of  Cat Lady and Lorelai
Lonely jobs have provided excellent material for independent video games over the years. From Papers, Please to Firewatch to The Stanley Parable, players have been happy to spend hours dwelling in depressing cubicles or rural hideaways, usually because there is an intriguingly hidden point to it all.
In Trainwatch, a character named Troy has taken a seemingly godforsaken job as a railway worker in an unnamed desolate backwater. His main task over the course of a single month is to manage a level crossing, closing the gate whenever a train comes, while also carrying out daily chores such as cooking and washing. It sounds serene, but Troy is also running away from something. The other stipulations are that he stays sober and calls his wife every night. articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.description:
An increasing tension between players and publishers about ownership of titles could lead to a divestment from the system the big companies are trying to enforce
At the time of press, there is a well-publicised protest taking place in the video games community. PlayStation 5 owners are being encouraged to log off from their consoles between 23 and 30 August – no playing games, no downloading new titles. The motivating factor is Sony’s decision to cease physical game disc production from January 2028. After that, games will only be released as digital products. In an act of poor timing or wilful defiance, Sony chose this week to send out a mass email reminding customers of their PS5 terms and conditions: “The software is licensed to you, not sold,” states the relevant clause. “You are granted a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, and personal license to play … ” It knows, of course, that most customers won’t open the email, let alone read it.
There has always been a tension between game players and game publishers – an underlying sense of mutual mistrust. Players are wary of their favourite franchises being canned, or games being delayed or released with bugs. Publishers and manufacturers are wary of piracy and the capricious tastes of consumers. But now the atmosphere among many game players feels more starkly political than ever. Microsoft has been targeted by the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement for its ties to the Israeli military; the consumer advocacy group Stop Killing Games is gaining support; players have protested over the purchase of Electronic Arts by a Saudi-led consortium – boycotts have been proposed in part due to the possible ramifications regarding LGBTQ+ content in titles such as The Sims. As the games industry has grown and globalised, its impact on culture, society and politics has increased. Yet, on an individual level, gamers and consumers are feeling increasingly powerless.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: With the end of physical media in sight, gamers have had enough

Samsung’s latest folding phone breaks the mould with a squat, passport-like shape reminiscent of the Blackberry, which opens up to become a tablet similar to an iPad mini. It is certainly a better shape for a tablet than other designs, but is a short and wide phone when closed a compromise too far?
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is an entirely new variant in Samsung’s foldable family for this year launched alongside the Z Fold 8 Ultra with a more familiar candy bar shape. Both folders are extremely expensive, with the Fold 8 starting at £1,699 (€1,999/$1,899.99/A$2,699) and the Fold 8 Ultra at £1,899 (€2,199/$2,099.99/A$2,999), with RAMageddon driving up prices even at the top of the market.
